content: Medications should only be administered to patients who are not poisoned if deemed necessary. If the inquiry is better addressed by another organization, such as a rabies hotline, the caller should be provided with the appropriate contact number. All calls to the poisons information center must be documented in the poison information database either at the time of the call or as soon as possible afterward. The on-duty specialist in poisons information should enter the call details and finalize the documentation by 12:00 PM following the duty period. For teratology-related inquiries, designated resources and appropriate toxicology references should be used. When responding to callers, the information given should be tailored to the specific case and the caller’s background, whether they are a physician, nurse, or member of the general public. Detailed clinical information should not be shared with the general public, but basic information about symptoms indicating poisoning may be provided. First-aid advice, such as rinsing exposed skin, can be given. If there is a risk of poisoning, the caller should be referred to a doctor or hospital and advised whether an ambulance is necessary. Patients outside of a hospital setting may only require advice on referral to a healthcare facility. For medical personnel, the patient’s risk of toxicity should be assessed, and the caller should be informed of potential signs and symptoms, the timeframe for toxicity to manifest (including delayed effects), and any necessary clinical investigations, laboratory analyses, or antidote use criteria. It is essential to confirm that the caller has understood the information provided. A summary of the advice given, including any input from a consultant medical toxicologist, should be recorded in the appropriate section of the call record or database. While information is typically provided over the phone, it may sometimes be necessary to email relevant details to the caller. In such cases, a warning should be included, advising that the information is regularly updated and should not be archived. If a specialist in poisons information is uncertain about the advice to provide after consulting appropriate resources and colleagues, or if the inquiry is outside their expertise, or if the caller specifically requests to speak to a medical toxicologist, a referral should be made. In such cases, the caller should either be asked to wait while the case is discussed or informed that the consultant medical toxicologist will be contacted, and the caller will be updated. An example of an assessment record for evaluating the performance of a poisons information specialist is provided. This record should be adapted to the specific operations of the poison center. The assessment evaluates whether the reason for the call was ascertained, sufficient information was obtained, a risk assessment was conducted, a treatment plan was provided, specialist referral was offered when applicable, appropriate language was used for the caller’s level of understanding, and whether the caller received and understood sufficient information. Additionally, a user satisfaction questionnaire can be used to gather feedback from poison center users. This survey can be conducted using a paper form or online and should be tailored to the poison center’s operations. The questionnaire includes questions about the promptness of the response, the helpfulness and manner of the staff, satisfaction with the advice received, sufficiency of the information provided, confidence in the accuracy of the information, timeliness of the information, and willingness to use the service again. A section for free-text comments or suggestions is also included.
